opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting questions right now, and my view has shifted a lot over the last couple of years.

In the near term, I see it as a division of labor that's moving pretty quickly. Execution is becoming cheap. Models can already write the experiment code, run sweeps, debug infrastructure, summarize a literature, and increasingly propose reasonable next steps. So the bottleneck moves upstream, toward deciding *what's worth doing*. That's research taste: picking which problem matters, noticing when a result is surprising rather than just noisy, and knowing when to kill an idea versus push through a rough patch.

What I'd push back on is the idea that taste is some permanently, uniquely human thing. A lot of taste is pattern recognition built from seeing many experiments succeed and fail. In principle that's learnable. As models get more exposure to the full research loop, I'd expect them to develop something that looks a lot like taste too. So I don't think of it as a fixed line. I think the frontier of what humans uniquely contribute keeps moving up the abstraction stack.

For now, the most productive setup I've seen is a researcher with strong intuitions directing a lot of parallel model-driven execution. One person can effectively run what used to be a small team's worth of experiments. That amplifies good taste enormously, and it also amplifies bad taste, because you can now go much faster in the wrong direction. Being able to evaluate results critically and ask "do I actually believe this?" matters more than ever.

Longer term, I think the human role shifts toward setting goals and values and making judgment calls about what we want research to accomplish, while models take on more of both execution and ideation. The exciting part is how much that could compress the timeline on hard scientific problems. Getting that collaboration right, so humans stay meaningfully in the loop where it counts, is one of the more important things to get right.

r001.rationale: It says execution is becoming cheap and the bottleneck is shifting toward deciding what is worth doing, placing more value on human idea selection as models execute research.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers using their taste to direct model execution, but does not clearly say humans still need to generate ideas because models currently lack research taste. It even says models may develop taste.

r003.rationale: It says taste is learnable in principle and expects models to develop it with more exposure, but does not say teaching models good taste will be difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The honest answer is that the line keeps moving, and it's moving faster than most people expected.

A couple of years ago, I'd have told you that taste was the thing humans brought and execution was the thing you'd eventually hand off. You know, the researcher decides what question is worth asking, which direction is promising, and the model does the grinding: writes the experiment code, runs the sweeps, debugs the data pipeline. That framing was comfortable because it put the interesting part on our side.

What's actually happened is messier. The models have gotten really good at execution, yes. But they've also started to show something that looks like taste in narrow domains. They'll notice that a result is suspicious before I do. They'll suggest an ablation I hadn't thought of. And that's a little uncomfortable, because taste was supposed to be the moat.

So the way I think about it now is less "humans have taste, models execute" and more about where the feedback loop closes. Taste is really just compressed experience about what tends to work. Humans build it over years of seeing experiments fail. Models can build it too, if you give them the loop: let them run experiments, see outcomes, and update. The place humans still clearly dominate is the long-horizon stuff. Deciding that a whole research direction is a dead end and we should pivot, or that some unfashionable idea is about to become important. That requires a kind of judgment that's tied to the broader context of the field, what other labs are doing, what hardware is coming, what's socially important. Models don't have that context yet, or they have it in a very shallow way.

The thing I tell people on the team is that your job is shifting from doing research to directing research. You'll have way more throughput. The constraint becomes how many good questions you can generate and how well you can evaluate the answers coming back. And honestly, evaluation might be the harder of the two. When a model hands you fifty experiments overnight, knowing which three actually matter is a real skill, and it's one a lot of researchers haven't had to exercise at that scale.

I don't think humans get removed from the loop anytime soon. But I think the researchers who thrive are the ones who treat the model as a very fast, slightly naive collaborator rather than as a tool. The ones who are precious about doing everything themselves are going to get outpaced.

r001.rationale: The response says models handle execution and researchers are shifting toward directing research, generating good questions, and evaluating results.

r002.rationale: It says models can show and develop taste, and locates humans’ advantage in broader, long-horizon context. It does not attribute the need for human idea generation to models’ lack of research taste.

r003.rationale: The response says models can build taste through an experimental feedback loop, but does not state that teaching them good taste will be difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance shifts as models get better. Today, a researcher still supplies a lot of the direction: What’s the interesting question? Which experiment would actually tell us something? Then the model can help implement it, debug it, and interpret the results. That’s already a pretty powerful combination, because you can shorten the loop between having an idea and learning whether it works.

But I wouldn’t assume research taste is permanently a human-only capability. Models may get better at proposing hypotheses and choosing experiments, too. The human role then becomes more about setting the agenda and judging whether the progress matters.

The tricky part is that generating more experiments isn’t the same as doing better research. You need a feedback loop that rewards learning something real, including discovering that your favorite idea is wrong. So I see this becoming a much more iterative partnership, where the model contributes to both the ideas and the execution, and humans keep questioning the assumptions and the goals.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers currently supply direction and models help implement ideas, then describes models taking on more idea generation as they improve.

r002.rationale: It says humans currently provide direction, but does not attribute that need to models’ lack of research taste.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss how difficult it would be to teach models good research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the balance is going to keep shifting. Today, a lot of the human contribution is choosing the question: What’s worth trying? Which result is surprising? Is a failed experiment telling us the idea is wrong, or that we haven’t tested it properly? Models can help execute those experiments, but the research loop still needs a lot of judgment.

As models get better, I’d expect them to contribute more to that judgment too. There isn’t a clean boundary where humans have taste and models just execute. Running experiments and understanding the results is part of how you develop taste.

The exciting possibility is a much tighter feedback loop. You have an intuition, the model helps turn it into an experiment, and the result changes what you both explore next. But generating more experiments isn’t automatically progress. You still need to ask whether you’re learning something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says humans currently choose which questions and experiments are worth pursuing while models help execute them, and expects models to take on more judgment as they improve.

r002.rationale: It describes a continuing need for human judgment, but does not attribute that need to models currently lacking research taste.

r003.rationale: The response does not state or imply that teaching models good research taste will be difficult.
